paragraphs: A ready group of studio microphones spares you from building a recording booth one piece at a time. Condenser capsules, mesh grilles and elastic shock mounts are the parts that read first when the camera moves close to a vocal setup. Each microphone keeps its own silhouette, so a row of them on stands never looks like copies of one object.

The bundle passed CheckMate Pro inspection, the strictest tier TurboSquid applies to naming, scale and file structure. That matters in a set, because you will often pull a single mic out and place it on a desk or boom arm. Chrome bodies and dark grilles also give a lighting artist strong contrast to play with in a dim studio.

Three versions of the bundle sit side by side, and each carries a different selection of microphones. The main set costs $69, Collection 4 sells for $59, and the larger Collection 2 goes for $119. On sale since 2016, these mics still dress podcast rooms, radio stations, music videos and audio gear product shots.

A single canopy lowering a cargo pallet shows how heavy loads drift down after release, ready for space recovery and airdrop sequences. Its 156,826 polygons and 158,366 vertices go into the dome, the fabric gores and the long rigging lines that converge on the payload. Those thin lines keep their profile even when the camera follows the descent from directly below.

Fabric panels sit on a non-overlapping UV layout, so each gore can take its own stitching or scorch marks without mirrored seams. Construction follows the CheckMate specification, which means frozen transforms, sensible naming and a hierarchy that opens without surprises. The bell shape and the hanging payload give an animator a clear pivot for a gentle pendulum swing.

Three versions are offered, all at $59, so the choice is about color and layout rather than budget. Alongside the main model come a white subscale cargo system and a yellow subscale canopy carrying its own payload. Released in 2024, the parachute suits aerospace explainers, documentary reconstructions and mission animations.

These raw ore nuggets have rough, pitted faces that catch light in every crease, forming a convincing pile of treasure. The whole cluster stays at 5,415 polygons and 5,423 vertices, so dozens of copies can fill a mine floor without slowing the viewport. Irregular facets replace smooth pebble shapes, which is what makes the lumps read as freshly extracted metal.

Each stone sits on its own non-overlapping UV island, letting you vary tarnish, dirt or polish between neighbors. Assembly follows CheckMate rules, so the file opens at consistent scale with tidy object names. Scattered on velvet or dumped in a mine cart, the nuggets hold up from both close and distant cameras.

Natural Minerals Big Stones comes in three metal finishes, so the same shapes can play gold, silver or copper. The gold set and the silver variant cost $59 each, while the copper version is priced at $49. Offered since 2021, they fit fantasy loot, mining games, museum displays and finance stories about precious metals.

A mechanical hand raising one finger gives sci-fi scenes a clear gesture for pointing, pressing a switch or signaling a pause. Of its 118,854 polygons over 61,295 vertices, most sit in the knuckle joints and the plated segments of each digit. Visible actuators and gaps between plates make it read as a machine rather than a gloved human hand.

Panel wear, scratches and glowing strips can be painted freely, since the UV islands never overlap. StemCell delivery keeps the same PBR materials consistent across several renderers without manual rebuilding. Brushed metal on the fingers against darker joints gives the hand strong readable contrast under studio light.

Three variants share one price of $59 and differ in pose and coverage. Besides the one-finger gesture you can choose a full futuristic humanoid robot arm or a robot hand holding a two-finger pose. Available since 2023, the hand suits game cinematics, technology explainers and artificial intelligence key art.

This rail launcher hangs beneath a fighter wing to carry and fire short range missiles, delivered here as a compact pylon component. Its 18,990 polygons and 20,155 vertices cover the rail grooves, access panels and fastener rows along the slim body. A tapered nose and flat mounting face show exactly how the unit bolts to the wing station above.

Stenciled markings, chipped paint and grease streaks fit onto non-overlapping UVs without mirrored text on the far side. Because it follows the CheckMate specification, the launcher lines up cleanly when attached to an existing aircraft. Gray military paint over a narrow body keeps it believable whether it is loaded or empty on the rail.

Three choices are available for this hardware, and two of them share the base price of $59. The plain Missile Launcher LAU-129 and a generic aircraft missile launcher cost $59, while the version with its mount costs $69. First released in 2024, it serves flight simulators, military training material, games and aviation documentaries.

Stacked shipping containers joined by stairs and walkways form a ready field base for any compact military or industrial compound. The budget is heavy at 1,121,846 polygons and 1,106,784 vertices, spent on corrugated walls, railings, door locks and stair treads. Spanning 744.21 x 487.86 x H579.2 cm, it scales correctly next to soldiers, trucks and other props.

Green paint can age unevenly across each box, since the UV islands are laid out without overlaps. Built to CheckMate rules, the structure keeps predictable names and pivots when you split the stack apart. Railings and stair runs give characters obvious routes to climb between the levels.

Three structure versions come at the same price of $59 apiece, each with its own color and layout. Next to the green military assembly you will find a white multi-tier container scaffold and a gray two-level industrial access platform. Released in 2025, they suit war games, construction sites, logistics hubs and post-apocalyptic environments.

A worn brown leather flight jacket with a shearling collar brings instant character to a pilot, a biker or a wardrobe still life. Its 91,901 polygons over 46,724 vertices go into creased sleeves, a heavy zipper and the thick fur lining folded over the shoulders. Creases fall where real leather bends, at the elbows and under the arms, so the garment never looks freshly pressed.

Scuffs and faded patches can vary panel by panel, thanks to UVs that never overlap. The jacket passed CheckMate Pro inspection, a sign of clean geometry and a well organized file. Dark fur against brown leather gives two very different surfaces for a lighting artist to separate.

Real Leather Aviator Jacket Brown Old Fur is one of three jacket versions offered, each costing $59. The alternatives are a brown leather bomber with fur and a shabby black men's aviator jacket. In the catalog since 2023, it fits period films, character dressing, fashion renders and military history scenes.

A light tube of stretch fabric pulled over the neck and chin, this gaiter dresses runners, cyclists and outdoor characters simply. Modeled in 6,398 polygons and 6,532 vertices, it shows soft folds where the fabric bunches below the jaw. That small count lets you add it to a character without loading the scene with extra cloth detail.

Printed patterns or a knitted texture can wrap the whole tube, because the UV islands sit apart. CheckMate Pro certification stands behind the piece, so scale and structure stay consistent across its formats. The open top edge and the gathered lower rim make it easy to fit over different neck shapes.

Three gaiter versions share a single price of $59, differing only in their print. Alongside the summer Neck Gaiter there is a multifunctional gaiter in camouflage and another in plain blue. Selling since 2021, the design serves sportswear catalogs, hiking characters, pandemic-era scenes and tactical outfits.

A realistic East Asian male head with a facial rig lets you animate expressions for dialogue, medical training or character previews. Proportions of the cheekbones, eyelids and jaw are shaped with care, since small shifts there change how a face reads. The built-in rig moves the mouth and brows, so expressions need no hand-sculpted shapes.

Clean edge loops around the eyes and lips keep deformation smooth once the controls start driving them. CheckMate Pro status confirms that topology, naming and scale follow strict rules, which matters on a head meant to deform. A calm neutral expression at rest gives a clean starting point before any animation is applied.

Three builds of the Asian Male Head 2 Rigged 3D Model share one price of $49. Besides the main head, there are two alternatives prepared for specific software, one rigged for Maya and one rigged for Cinema 4D. First released in 2015, it is still chosen for anatomy lessons, games and digital human tests.

A large digital mixing desk with lit screens and rows of motorized faders anchors any live sound or broadcast booth scene. It is dense at 352,654 polygons over 180,751 vertices, with most of that going into knobs, buttons and fader caps. The illuminated display and colored channel strips show the desk powered on, which helps a concert shot feel alive.

Its UV layout uses overlapping islands, so repeated controls share texture space and the maps stay compact. StemCell delivery carries the same materials across renderers, which saves time when moving between engines. The sloped control surface and raised meter bridge give the desk a strong profile from the engineer's seat.

Three console versions come at an identical price of $49, so you choose by look alone. Pick the Behringer x32 digital Mixer Switched, a generic digital mixing audio console or a Behringer x32 shown as a plain mixing console. Available since 2024, it suits concert stages, recording studios, church sound booths and music videos.

A full-face racing helmet with a smooth shell and dark visor is ready to sit on a rider or rest on a garage shelf. Its 50,501 polygons over 27,277 vertices keep the curved shell clean and the vents sharp around the chin bar. The visor pivot and the padded liner seen through the opening give it the weight of real protective gear.

Decals, race numbers or scratches can run across the shell without mirroring, as each UV island has its own space. The file carries CheckMate Pro status, meaning it is tidy, correctly scaled and ready for production pipelines. The matte grey paint shows reflections softly, so studio lighting traces the shell's curves without harsh glare.

Two other helmet versions join this grey racing shell, and all three cost the same $49. You can choose a colorful motorcycle helmet or an Icon Airflite helmet in a quicksilver finish. Released in 2023, the Bike Racing Helmet Grey serves motocross games, rider characters, product renders and racing animations.

A soft military field cap with fold-down earflaps keeps a soldier or a hunter dressed for cold weather. Built from 22,798 polygons and 25,793 vertices, it shows stitched seams, a stiff peak and two flaps buttoned up over the crown. The fabric sags slightly at the sides, which keeps it from looking like a rigid plastic shell.

It ships with 5 textures at 2048 x 2048, laid onto non-overlapping UVs so stitching and wear do not mirror between sides. Its CheckMate Lite rating confirms basic geometry and file standards for everyday production use. Dark wool tones absorb light, so the stitching lines give the cap most of its visible detail.

Three cap versions share this cut with the flaps, and every one of them costs $49. The black Field Cap with Earflaps is joined by an olive green cap and a camo cap. Offered since 2019, the caps suit army characters, hunting scenes, winter outfits and historical reenactment renders.

Every tool a bartender reaches for sits on one stand here, from shakers and jiggers to strainers, spoons and a muddler. All 21 pieces together come to 34,423 polygons and 33,841 vertices, so each tool stays light while the set still reads complete. The twisted bar spoon handle and the coiled spring of the strainer are what a close shot picks up first.

Separate UV space for each tool lets you add its own polish, fingerprints or water spots without repeats. Following CheckMate rules, pivots and names are organized so you can lift any single item off the stand. Bright steel against a dark bar counter makes the whole kit catch highlights in moody lighting.

Three versions of the Complete Bartender Kit 21 Pieces Stainless Steel cost $49 each, differing in finish. Beside the steel kit you can pick copper tools on a wooden stand or a gold kit on that same stand. Selling since 2021, the set fits bar interiors, cocktail recipe videos and kitchenware catalogs.

A weather satellite with twin solar wings and a sensor deck aimed at the planet, shaped for orbital shots and climate science explainers. It carries 123,485 polygons and 130,219 vertices across the bus, the instrument housings and the gridded solar arrays. Scaled to real-world size, it sits comfortably beside other spacecraft in an orbital scene.

Foil wrinkles and panel cells can vary over the whole body, because the UV islands stay separate. The CheckMate specification guided the build, so parts are named and grouped for animating the arrays as they unfold. Gold insulation against dark solar cells gives the spacecraft strong color contrast against a black sky.

The GOES-R Satellite Double Panel is one of three spacecraft versions offered together. It and a geostationary operational environmental satellite cost $49 each, while a meteorological monitoring satellite costs $39. Introduced in 2025, the satellite fits space documentaries, weather broadcasts, educational animations and science museum displays.

A wedge-shaped handheld console with two screens set in one flat slab, the Nintendo 2DS suits retro gaming shelves and bedroom scenes. Its 19,415 polygons and 20,334 vertices cover the sloped body, the circle pad, the face buttons and the hinge-free shell. That slanted profile is what a viewer recognizes first, so it is modeled with crisp edges.

It comes with 19 textures at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 for clean button labels and screen art. Those maps sit on non-overlapping UVs, and CheckMate Pro approval vouches for an accurate, orderly file. The bright plastic shell suits soft daylight, which keeps a bedroom or desk scene relaxed.

Three entries are available at $49 apiece: the main console, a handheld game console variant and a second version of the same handheld. Its license is Editorial Uses Only, so it belongs in articles, reviews, documentaries and news illustrations about portable gaming. Collectors and writers have been able to pick up this handheld model since 2017.

Chunky men's running sneakers with a mesh upper and layered suede overlays show the texture of a modern trainer up close. The pair spends 64,270 polygons over 53,230 vertices on stitched panels, lace eyelets and the cushioned midsole. A fur-like lining around the collar is what separates these shoes from a standard running model.

Wear on the toe box and heel can differ between left and right, since no UV islands overlap. A CheckMate Pro rating keeps scale and structure consistent across every format in the download. Soft suede and coarse mesh sit side by side, giving close renders two contrasting surfaces to light.

New Balance Mens Sneakers Fur comes in three versions, each priced at $49: this pair, black core sneakers and another fur pair. Available since 2023, the shoes carry an Editorial Uses Only license for reviews, news stories and fashion journalism. That lets a style column or a shoe review show real footwear without rebuilding it.

A forestry safety helmet with an attached mesh visor and earmuffs, built for chainsaw work and logging scenes in the woods. Its 143,138 polygons over 72,158 vertices go into the vented shell, the folding face guard and the padded hearing protectors. Visor hinges and earmuff arms are separate, so a close shot shows how the system really attaches.

The bright shell can collect sap stains, dust and scuffs freely, because its UV islands are kept apart. Checked against CheckMate Pro rules, the file meets strict standards for geometry and naming. The fine visor mesh is what sells the helmet as real gear when light passes through it.

The Orange Helmet Head comes with two sibling versions at the same $49: a yellow-orange protective helmet and a Husqvarna forest helmet. Sold since 2022 with Editorial Uses Only terms, it fits safety guides, news images and documentary forestry scenes.

A packed set of picnic gear lets you lay out a blanket scene in minutes, with baskets, plates and food ready to arrange. It gathers props that usually take hours to model one by one, from a wicker basket to cups and serving pieces. The objects are sized to work together, so the spread looks natural when the camera looks down at the blanket.

Every object here meets CheckMate Pro requirements for naming and scale, so pieces can be pulled out individually. Woven textures and painted ceramics give the set a warm, handmade feel suited to sunny afternoon light.

Three Picnic Accesories Collection versions exist, each with its own selection of items. The main set costs $49, Collection 2 is priced at $69, and the largest, Collection 3, costs $129. Released in 2021, it serves park scenes, lifestyle images, summer animations and food styling layouts.

A dual-slot workstation graphics card with a sealed cooler shroud and blower fan fits PC builds and hardware explainers. Its 84,105 polygons and 88,565 vertices go into the fan blades, heatsink fins and gold contacts of the PCIe connector. Display outputs on the bracket are modeled individually, so a rear view holds up too.

It ships with 7 textures at 4096 x 4096, enough for small print on the board and clean metal finishes. Those maps rest on non-overlapping UVs, and the card holds a CheckMate Lite rating. Its flat shroud gives a calm surface that photographs well against a dark motherboard.

Two siblings come with the Professional Graphic Video Card, all at $49: a card labeled Nvidia Quadro and a Nvidia Quadro GV100. Selling since 2019, it suits computer build guides, tech reviews, server room scenes and online store images. Each version keeps the same compact dual-slot proportions, so swapping between them changes only the labeling.

A slim LED smart TV on a compact stand dresses living rooms, hotel suites and electronics store shelves with a believable screen. The Samsung LED H5203 Series Smart TV inch uses 36,641 polygons and 38,264 vertices for the thin bezel, the stand and rear ports. Its flat front accepts any image you place on the screen for a broadcast or game shot.

It includes 9 textures at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048, which keep the logo and port labels sharp. Its geometry passed CheckMate Pro review, and the UV islands are laid out without overlaps. A black glossy frame reflects room lights, so it reads as switched off unless you add screen content.

Three screen sizes are available, each for $49: the base model plus a 50 inch and a 46 inch version. Since 2016 it has been offered under Editorial Uses Only terms, suited to news stories, reviews and documentary interiors.

Rotting zombie hands reaching up with clawed fingers suit graveyards, horror games and Halloween shots where the dead break through soil. They are modeled in 9,526 polygons and 9,569 vertices, light enough to place many of them in one crowd. Torn skin, exposed knuckles and long cracked nails make the reaching gesture read clearly even from a distance.

They arrive with 5 textures at 4096 x 4096, so bruised skin and dried blood hold up in close shots. Separate UV islands and a CheckMate Pro rating back up a clean layout and well organized geometry. Gray-green skin tones blend well with mud, fog and moonlight in a night scene.

Scary Zombie Hands is one of three versions sharing the $49 price. The others are a pair of zombie arms frozen in an attack pose and a pair of horror zombie arms. First listed in 2019, they work for horror films, haunted house attractions, game levels and Halloween decor.

A seated bronze figure with chin resting on hand, this famous sculpture adds a contemplative accent to museums, gardens and libraries. The Thinker Statue holds 26,410 polygons over 13,248 vertices, enough for tense back muscles and curled toes gripping the rock. The pose leans forward heavily over the knee, so the silhouette reads well from almost any side of the plinth.

A patina can pool in the deep folds without repeating patterns, since UV islands do not overlap. CheckMate Pro approval indicates the sculpture is properly scaled and neatly organized. Raking side light brings out the muscles best, which is how museums usually show the original.

Three materials are available for the same seated figure, priced at $49 each. You can choose the bronze statue, a white gypsum cast or a polished marble version of the same pose. Offered since 2022, it suits gallery scenes, philosophy illustrations, campus renders and classical interior design.

An empty seminar room with plain white walls is a clean shell to furnish for training sessions, workshops or office presentations. It is very light at 3,207 polygons and 3,581 vertices, since the budget covers only walls, ceiling, floor and window openings. That leaves the scene free for chairs, desks, projection screens and plants of your own choosing.

Baked lighting and floor patterns fit neatly onto the surfaces, because the UV islands are kept separate. StemCell delivery means the materials work across several renderers without any manual setup. Daylight through the windows falls across the bare floor, which gives the empty space a calm and open mood.

Training Seminar Room Empty White has two sibling versions, and all three cost $49. The alternatives are a conference room with no furniture at all and a blue empty seminar room. Available since 2023, the rooms serve architectural visualization, e-learning videos, virtual events and corporate interiors.

An old-style studio microphone on a tall stand recalls radio broadcasts, crooners and jazz club stages from past decades. Its 74,811 polygons and 75,101 vertices give the grille its fine mesh and the stand its threaded joints. A heavy round base keeps the silhouette grounded and makes the prop believable on a stage.

Chrome pitting, worn paint and dust in crevices fit onto UV islands that never overlap. The CheckMate specification guided its construction, keeping names and pivots consistent for quick placement in a scene. Under a single warm spotlight the chrome head throws bright highlights that read well against dark backdrops.

The Vintage Studio Microphone on Stand shares one $49 price with two condenser versions. One is a generic condenser microphone with stand, and the other is a Rode condenser microphone with stand. Released in 2024, the vintage mic fits music videos, retro radio scenes, podcast sets and small concert stages.

A group of desktop globes on stands, from wooden cradles to metal arms, dresses studies, classrooms and travel scenes. The globes differ in base shape and meridian ring design, so a shelf of them never looks repetitive. Each sphere sits on its own axis, so you can spin it in an animation without rebuilding the stand.

All pieces pass CheckMate Pro standards for scale and naming, so you can pull a single globe out for desk dressing. Printed continents and ocean blues give each sphere strong color, even when it is small in the frame. Brass and wood stands also give a library interior an instant feel of age and study.

Three versions of the World Globes with Stand Collection are available, each with a different selection of models. The main collection costs $49, Collection 2 costs $59 and Collection 3 is priced at $69. In the catalog since 2022, the globes suit libraries, school interiors, office desks and geography explainers.

A carved hand drum with a goblet body and tensioned rope lacing brings rhythm and folk craft into music and travel scenes. Its 46,862 polygons over 23,699 vertices go mostly into the rope netting and the carved patterns around the body. The stretched skin head shows the slight dome that real hide forms under tension.

Wood grain and the painted motif can differ on each side of the drum, since the UVs never overlap. Passing CheckMate Pro review confirms that geometry, naming and scale meet high standards. The narrow waist between bowl and foot is the shape players grip between their knees.

African Drum with Folk Motif comes with two other drum versions, all three at $39. You can choose an ornate African djembe with richer carving or a plainer djembe drum. On offer since 2023, it works for music scenes, cultural documentaries, festival sets and souvenir shop interiors.

A curved gaming tower with a glowing front ring and side window shows the look of a high-end desktop PC in any setup. It holds 306,017 polygons over 159,114 vertices, most of them in the vent mesh, the angled panels and the rear ports. Its rounded shell and lighting strip are the features a viewer identifies immediately.

Dust, fingerprints and glossy reflections can be added without mirrored seams, because no UV islands overlap. The tower earned CheckMate Pro status, which speaks to clean topology and tidy structure. In a dark room the glowing ring becomes the brightest point in the frame and pulls the eye.

Of the three versions, the white Alienware Aurora Gaming Desktop costs $39, while a black Aurora and a red liquid cooled desktop cost $59. Sold since 2023, it is licensed as Editorial Uses Only, which limits it to reviews, news stories and gaming editorials.

A steel 50L beer keg fitted with a picnic tap and CO2 regulator is ready for bar cellars, parties and brewery scenes. Its 30,350 polygons and 31,097 vertices form the ribbed keg body, the coupler and the hose running to the hand tap. A small gas cylinder beside it shows how the system pushes beer out of the keg.

Dents, scratches and condensation can be painted onto the steel without repeats, since the UVs are non-overlapping. As a CheckMate Pro asset, it arrives with clean geometry and organized files. Brushed steel bands around the keg catch light in rings, which makes the cylinder read clearly.

Beer Keg 50L with Leland CO2 Picnic Tap comes in three versions, all priced at $39. The others are a 50L keg with a portable tap and a 30L steel keg using the Leland setup. Selling since 2020, it fits brewery interiors, backyard parties, bar storage rooms and food service renders.

Glossy black tap dancing shoes with metal plates on the toe and heel suit dance studios, stage shows and costume scenes. They hold 76,636 polygons over 41,096 vertices, mostly in the laces, stitching and the screws that fix the taps to the sole. The low heel and rounded toe give them the classic profile that dancers recognize at a glance.

Leather scuffs and polished taps can be textured separately, as the UV islands stay apart. The pair carries a CheckMate Pro rating, a mark of clean geometry and correct scale. Patent leather mirrors stage lights strongly, so even a dim scene shows the shoes' shape.

Tap Shoes come in three versions at $39: this black pair, a white and black pair and a gold pair. Released in 2023, they suit dance school interiors, musical theater scenes, costume catalogs and retro performance shots. The gold version in particular catches spotlights and suits glamorous revue costumes on a bright stage.

A stylized cartoon Moon with soft craters and a rounded surface brings a friendly look to children's animations and space games. It uses only 2,568 polygons and 2,524 vertices, smooth enough for close shots yet light enough for mobile games and VR. Craters are wide and shallow, so they read clearly even when the Moon is small in the frame.

Simple gradients or hand drawn textures can be painted across the surface on non-overlapping UVs. It qualifies for CheckMate Pro, so topology and scale meet the standard production pipelines expect. Pale gray tones keep it calm next to brighter cartoon planets in the same sky.

Cartoon Planet Moon has two companion versions in the same playful style, Mercury and Neptune, each costing $39. Available since 2022, the set works for kids' shows, educational apps, space-themed games and storybook illustrations. Several of them together can form a small, charming solar system for a classroom animation.

A PDC drill bit with cutter-studded blades shows how oil and gas wells are bored through rock, ideal for technical visuals. Its 37,457 polygons and 37,544 vertices cover the curved blades, round diamond cutters, nozzle ports and the junk slots between them. A threaded shank at the back shows how the bit couples to the drill string.

Grit, mud and wear on the cutters fit onto separate UV islands without visible repetition. It was assembled to CheckMate specification, keeping names and pivots consistent across the file. Spiraling blades around the face make the bit look ready to spin, even in a static render.

The Drilling Rig Bit PDC is offered in three versions at $39 each: standard, gold and blue. Introduced in 2024, it fits energy industry explainers, oil rig scenes, engineering presentations and trade show renders. The colored finishes help a featured bit stand apart from the gray steel equipment around it on a rig floor.

A padded medical exam table with a raised backrest gives clinic and doctor's office scenes their central piece of furniture. Its 11,347 polygons and 11,808 vertices shape the cushioned top, the steel frame and the step that patients climb onto. Stitched seams along the vinyl upholstery keep it from reading as a plain block when the camera comes close.

It is textured with 4 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048, enough to show vinyl grain and scuffed metal. StemCell delivery means those materials open correctly across the main renderers without manual rewiring. Pale upholstery under cool overhead light gives the examination room the clean, clinical mood people expect.

Three versions share the $39 price: the main Exam Table 3D Model, a second build under the same name and a medical examination chair. First offered in 2016, the table still dresses hospital corridors, medical training videos, health explainers and pharmacy interiors.

A rugged diving watch with a round bezel and chunky buttons, built for underwater sports scenes and outdoor product shots. Garmin Descent G1 Black spends 196,304 polygons over 98,891 vertices on the knurled bezel, the strap holes and the button guards. The thick silicone strap and wide case give it the tough, tool-like look divers trust.

Watch faces, scratches and strap textures can be painted with no mirroring, as every UV island is laid apart. Inspected at CheckMate Pro level, the file arrives clean, correctly scaled and logically named. Matte black surfaces soak up light, so rim lighting is the best way to bring out its silhouette.

Three watch versions cost $39 each: this black Descent, a sport smartwatch with a red band and a Hurricane Blue solar edition. Selling since 2023, it fits diving scenes, fitness app mockups, outdoor gear catalogs and adventure films.

A round smartwatch with a flat glass face and slim sport band, shown here in its larger case size. The watch holds 31,778 polygons over 16,313 vertices across the case, the side keys and the band. The gently domed glass and the thin bezel are what make it read as a modern wearable at a glance.

Watch faces of your own design can be applied easily, because each part has its own UV space. TurboSquid certified it CheckMate Pro, which points to accurate proportions and tidy file structure. Graphite metal reflects soft studio light evenly, so the case looks finished without much tweaking.

Three finish versions are available at $39 each: graphite, sapphire and silver. On sale since 2023 under Editorial Uses Only, it suits tech reviews, news coverage and editorial lifestyle images. Wrist-level close-ups for a review article work well, since the band curves naturally around an arm shape.

An indoor rowing machine with a sliding seat, foot plates and a flywheel housing brings a home gym or fitness club to life. Its 75,013 polygons and 76,330 vertices go into the long monorail, the handle chain and the vented fan cover at the front. The low, stretched profile makes it instantly recognizable even when placed at the back of a busy gym.

Rubber grips, scuffed plastic and metal rails can be textured separately, because each UV island has room of its own. The machine holds a CheckMate Pro rating, so the file is consistent and properly scaled. A rower placed beside a window catches light along the rail, which helps the long shape read.

Three rower versions sell for $39 each: this indoor machine, a wooden rowing simulator and a water rowing machine for home use. Offered since 2023, they furnish home workout rooms, fitness studios, sports equipment catalogs and health videos.

A flowering mallow plant with white blooms and broad lobed leaves softens garden beds, cottage borders and window boxes. Malva Snow White uses 176,558 polygons and 160,736 vertices, spent on the open petals, the veined leaves and the branching stems. Each blossom faces a slightly different direction, which keeps the cluster from looking cloned.

Leaf veins and petal translucency can be painted precisely, since the plant's UV islands are all separate. StemCell delivery lets the foliage materials move between renderers without being rebuilt by hand. Backlit by low sun, the thin white petals glow and give a garden shot its warmth.

Three plant versions sell for $39: Malva Snow White, a mallow plant and a country mallow flower. Available since 2020, the mallow suits landscape design, garden visualization, nature scenes and botanical illustrations. Mixing the three versions in one bed produces a natural looking border without repeating a single specimen.

A smart street bin with a solar panel on its lid compacts trash and recyclables, ideal for modern plazas and city sidewalks. Its 28,706 polygons and 29,218 vertices shape the boxy body, the pull-down hoppers and the angled photovoltaic top. Separate openings for waste streams make the purpose of the unit readable from across a street scene.

It ships with 12 textures at 2048 x 2048, covering the painted metal, the solar cells and the recycling labels. Rated CheckMate Pro, the file is cleanly structured, with every UV island laid out on its own. Placed near benches and lamp posts, it signals a modern, well-run public space without drawing attention.

Three bin versions are offered for $39 each, including a generic solar smart bin and a Montclair solar powered trash bin. Since 2018 the Modern Solar Recycling Bin has dressed urban design renders, smart city presentations and sustainability explainers.

A rectangular tin of olive oil with a pour spout and handle fits pantry shelves, deli counters and Mediterranean kitchens.
